defaults.permitted_development: A side extension in England can be permitted development under Class A if it stays single storey, does not project in front of the principal elevation and is no more than half the width of the original house. Flats, maisonettes, listed buildings and homes with removed rights do not get the same fallback. Councils usually focus on whether the work stays subordinate to the original building and avoids an overbearing effect on neighbours.

rules.height_rules: For the usual permitted development route, a side extension should remain single storey, stay within a 4m overall height and keep eaves at or below 3m where any part is within 2m of a boundary.
rules.depth_rules: There is no separate side-extension depth allowance beyond the wider Class A limits, but the rear projection should stay modest enough that the scheme still reads as a side addition rather than a large rear extension.
rules.boundary_rules: Width and boundary siting are the main practical checks. The extension should stay no more than half the width of the original house, remain behind the principal elevation and avoid creating an overbearing flank wall beside neighbours or a highway. Councils usually focus on whether the work stays subordinate to the original building and avoids an overbearing effect on neighbours.
rules.roof_rules: The roof should stay clearly subordinate to the main house and within the overall height limit. Simple roofs that reduce bulk at the side boundary are usually easiest to justify.
rules.materials_rules: External materials should match or closely resemble the existing house so the side extension reads as part of the original building rather than a bolt-on addition. Councils usually focus on whether the work stays subordinate to the original building and avoids an overbearing effect on neighbours.

rules.permitted_development: In Broxbourne, the usual Class A route only works where the side addition stays single storey, remains behind the front wall and clearly passes the half-width test without swallowing the side passage that gives the house breathing space.

rules.height_rules: In Broxbourne, 4m overall and 3m to the eaves near the boundary are only the starting point; disciplined eaves and a low side roof usually matter more because they keep access and parking arrangements workable.
rules.depth_rules: Depth is judged less by a fixed metre rule than by whether the extension remains clearly subsidiary to the original side wall and does not read as an overlarge flank addition.
rules.boundary_rules: In Broxbourne, the boundary test usually comes down to whether a usable side route survives and whether the flank wall leaves neighbouring outlook or parking arrangements feeling squeezed.
rules.roof_rules: The roof should stay subordinate to the house and avoid creating a bulky flank mass. On taller side work, matching roof pitch and keeping the addition back from the front are usually critical design points.
rules.materials_rules: Use materials that tie the extension back to the original house, especially on prominent flank walls that are visible from the street. Councils usually focus on whether the work stays subordinate to the original building and avoids an overbearing effect on neighbours.

restrictions.conservation_area: Extensions in a conservation area often need a tighter design and siting assessment, especially on visible elevations or where the scheme would alter roof form, frontage or the rhythm of the street.
restrictions.listed_building: Do not rely on standard householder permitted development rights for a listed building. Listed building consent is usually required for works affecting character, and planning permission may also be needed.
restrictions.article4_notes: Article 4 directions can remove the usual householder fallback route in selected streets or heritage areas, so check the property's designation before relying on permitted development.
